concepts.title: What Economics Studies: The Ordinary Business of Life

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'What Economics Studies: The Ordinary Business of Life' refers to.
questions.a: Economics, as Alfred Marshall put it, studies man in the ordinary business of life -- how people earn, spend, save and choose among scarce means. Scarcity and choice form its core: unlimited wants chasing limited resources force every household, firm and government to economise.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'What Economics Studies: The Ordinary Business of Life'.
questions.a: Unlimited wants, limited resources -- every economic act is a choice about scarcity.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Economics Needs Statistics' refers to.
questions.a: Economic facts come as numbers -- prices, incomes, output, employment -- and statistics is the tool-set that collects, organises, presents, analyses and interprets them. Without statistical methods, the economist's statements would remain vague impressions instead of tested conclusions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Economics Needs Statistics'.
questions.a: Economics thinks in numbers -- statistics turns those numbers into evidence.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Why Economics Needs Statistics' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: The Three Central Problems of an Economy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Three Central Problems of an Economy' refers to.
questions.a: Every economy, rich or poor, must answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. Market economies answer through prices; centrally planned economies through state decisions; mixed economies blend both -- and statistics measures how well each answer works.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Three Central Problems of an Economy'.
questions.a: What, how, for whom -- three questions every economy must answer, by market or by plan.
